Home / Who it's for
For vendors

Your customer asked for an outside check. Here's what happens

A buyer, insurer or investor asked us to examine the evidence behind a claim you make. You'll be asked for that evidence and for written answers. The report goes only to the party who asked for the check.

What gets checked

One claim you make, and the evidence behind it

The party who asked names the claim and its scope: the version, the uses and the data it covers. That claim is what gets checked.

We examine your evidence for that claim. We don't examine your company, and we don't rate your product as a whole.

Claims that held

The Casebook counts 19 claims about AI products that held up, kept apart from the 139 cases where an AI error caused harm. A claim with sound evidence behind it is one a careful buyer can rely on.

The Casebook

How it works for you

Five things to know before it starts

This is what the party who asked will send you, what you will be asked for, your rights, and what the report contains.

2 · What you'll be asked for

  1. The claim, in writing, in the words you use to sell it.
  2. Its scope: which version, which uses, which data, and which people or cases it covers.
  3. The evidence behind it: test reports, the data or cases tested, and who ran the tests.
  4. Known limits and error rates, including any measured and not published.
  5. What changed in the product since those tests were run.

3 · Your rights

You answer every question in writing. You can't edit a finding. The report goes only to the party who asked for the check.

The examiner and the second reviewer write down their ties to you before work starts. We don't name a vendor beside a failure, and I won't publish a verdict on any named party.

4 · What the report contains

A private, signed report on each claim named:

  • The claim as examined, and its scope.
  • Finding 1: how far the evidence reaches, on a five-level scale.
  • Finding 2: whether any sound evidence, inside the claim's scope, shows the claim is false.
  • What's still open.
  • The ties the examiner and reviewer wrote down before work started.

The examiner signs it, and a second reviewer, independent of the examiner, releases it. See three sample reports.

Finding 1 uses five levels:

  1. Missing: The vendor gave no evidence for this claim.
  2. Shown to be flawed: The evidence has a defect that breaks it.
  3. Not enough to judge: There isn't enough evidence to decide either way.
  4. Sound, but short of the claim: The evidence holds up, but it supports less than the claim says.
  5. Sound, and reaching it: The evidence holds up and supports the whole claim.

The party who asked sets the level a claim must reach. For example: the claims the decision rests on must reach level 5.

The examiner must have shown practice checking software or systems against stated criteria: for example, an FAA software designee, an independent verification and validation engineer, or a test and evaluation engineer. That seat is being filled.

5 · Timing

The delivery date is set in writing with the party who asked, before work starts. The examiner's written questions come with a date to answer by.

If the evidence falls short

What the party who asked can do with it

If the evidence falls short, the party who asked decides what to do. These are the usual choices, so you know what is on the table.

WaitHold the award, the policy or the deal until there is evidence that reaches the claim.
Narrow the useRely on the product only where the evidence reaches, and write that limit down.
Accept the risk in writingGo ahead, and record what the evidence didn't cover, who accepted it, and why.
What it is not

It isn't a verdict on your company

An examination isn't a certification, and it isn't a verdict on your company. It's a written finding on the evidence behind one claim, for the scope named. We don't publish it.

Asked to take part in an examination?

Write to us with any question about the process, before or during the work.
